classification.difficultyReason: Count the shared fence once to construct the fencing constraint, distinguish one paddock's area from the total, and then apply the familiar quadratic maximisation procedure.

content.prompt: A farmer has 120 metres of fencing and needs to create two adjacent paddocks. These are identical rectangles that share a fence line on one side. What is the largest possible area of each paddock?

spec.sourceRegion: Question 4, right column, beneath the stem
spec.description: Two identical rectangular paddocks adjacent horizontally, with one vertical shared fence. The left paddock's bottom edge is labelled x and its outer left edge is labelled y. Decorative green background omitted; ordinary fences and labels use black.
spec.mathematics: Each paddock has width x and height y. The fence comprises four horizontal lengths x and three vertical lengths y, so 4x+3y=120.
spec.answerVisibility: Only supplied variables and fence geometry appear; no dimensions or maximum area are supplied.

answer.short:
$300\text{ m}^2$ for each paddock.

The area quadratic has its maximum halfway between its intercepts, giving $x=15\text{ m}$ and $y=20\text{ m}$.
answer.worked:
The shared fence is counted once. With $x,y>0$, the fencing constraint is
$$\begin{align*}
4x+3y&=120\\
y&=40-\frac{4}{3}x.
\end{align*}$$
The area $A$ of each paddock is
$$\begin{align*}
A&=xy\\
A&=x\left(40-\frac{4}{3}x\right)\\
A&=\frac{4}{3}x(30-x).
\end{align*}$$
This downward-opening quadratic has intercepts at $x=0$ and $x=30$, so its maximum occurs halfway between them:
$$\begin{align*}
x&=\frac{0+30}{2}=15\\
y&=40-\frac{4}{3}(15)=20\\
A_{\max}&=15\times20=300.
\end{align*}$$
The largest possible area of each paddock is $300\text{ m}^2$.
